newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - Tobacco stocks off after settlement.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Tobacco stocks off after settlement.

text.p: Shares in tobacco companies fell on Friday after the announcement of a landmark settlement reached between the industry, U.S. states and the public health community.
The following are analysts' comments on the news:
THOM BROWN, MANAGING DIRECTOR OF RUTHERFORD BROWN AND CATHERWOOD:
-- "My gut reaction is that it's going to cost the advertisers a lot of money. And in the long run it will cost the tobacco companies a lot of money."

-- "The dollar amount will make the profitability of the industry look very different for the next 25 years. There's a lot of cash flow in the industry, but if the whole world wakes up about the concerns about smoking like the U.S. has, it will be a field day for lawyers all over the world."
The agreement would require cigarette companies to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate states and smokers and to fund programs to help people quit smoking.
Philip Morris Cos Inc was off 1-1/2 to 46 in late trading. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp dipped 1-1/4 to 34-5/8.
Loews Corp, which owns Lorillard Tobacco Co, fell 3-1/4 to 103-3/8. UST Inc, owner of smokeless tobacco maker United States Tobacco Co, was off 1 to 29.
Gallaher Group Plc, a spinoff from American Brands, closed flat on the New York Stock Exchange at 19-3/8.
Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp's parent B.A.T Industries Plc was slightly higher, up 1/8 to 19-15/16.
Brooke Group Ltd, which owns Liggett Group Inc, inched upd 1/8 to 4-3/4.
BILL MEEHAN, MARKET ANALYST WITH PRUDENTIAL SECURITIES
-- "I think long-term it's positive for the group. There were expectations that the deal would be struck. The stocks were bidding up ahead on the rumor, so they're selling on the news."

-- "Certainty is always better than uncertainty. Philip Morris was trading at a multiple far less than it would have pretty much due to the uncertainty surrounding the litigation. This gets that uncertainty out of the way," Meehan said.
JOHN MCELROY III, PRINCIPAL, 1838 INVESTMENT ADVISORS LP

"I'm surprised the stocks are down. The key is, people can sue the industry in the future, but not for what's past. But I wonder if it will get through Congress like this, or if they will tinker with it.

"The industry has been incredibly clever at selling cigarettes and whatever restrictions they put on, the industry will probably keep some exposure to the public ... it will certainly slow down the growth, but they're pretty smart and you never know what might happen with growth overseas.
